Name: belief_time_indexing
Title: When Did You Believe It? Testing Whether LLMs Time-Index Their Beliefs About a Changing World
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's belief about a specific item is not just a truth-value but a time-indexed state: the same proposition can be true at time t1 and false at t2. We hypothesize that (a) LLMs internally represent a 'current-belief' distinct from 'stale/past-belief' states along a recoverable temporal-validity direction, (b) belief-vs-fact errors are partly errors of temporal indexing (the model reports a formerly-true state as currently believed), and (c) this temporal-validity direction is causally steerable to fix anachronistic belief reports without altering the underlying factual content.
Related Work: Suzgun et al. ('Belief in the Machine'/KaBLE) and the referenced paper 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' establish behavioral confusion but treat belief as an atemporal one-shot judgment. Truth-direction probing work (Marks & Tegmark; Savcisens & Eliassi-Rad 'Trilemma of Truth'; Schouten et al. on context-sensitive truth directions) recovers static veracity axes. Temporal-reasoning benchmarks (TempLAMA, TimeQA, situated/streaming updates) test factual recall over time behaviorally but do not probe or steer an internal *belief-time* representation, nor frame belief-vs-fact errors as temporal-indexing failures. My prior proposals covered agent-attribution, evidence-update inertia, and item-truth binding; none address the temporal dimension of belief validity. This recasts belief-vs-fact confusion as a temporal-indexing problem, a genuinely new lens.
Abstract: Beliefs about the world are time-indexed: a proposition true yesterday may be false today. Existing work shows LLMs conflate belief, knowledge, and fact, but treats an LLM's belief about an item as a single atemporal truth-value. We instead ask whether LLMs internally represent *when* a belief holds, and whether belief-vs-fact errors are partly failures of temporal indexing, i.e., reporting a formerly-true state as currently believed. Using controlled state-change narratives (an item's state changes across explicit timestamps or events, e.g., 'The vault held gold; last week it was emptied'), we query the model's belief about the item's state at the current time vs. earlier times, across several open-weight models. We train linear probes to recover (a) the state-value the model assigns and (b) the temporal validity index (current vs. stale). We find that current- and stale-belief states are separable along a recoverable temporal-validity direction, that anachronistic-belief errors (asserting an outdated state as current) coincide with collapse of this separation in deeper layers, and that causal steering along the temporal-validity direction shifts the model between current and past belief reports without changing the encoded state content. We introduce an anachronism-rate metric and show it grows with the number of state changes and narrative length, and that a lightweight steering/LoRA intervention reduces anachronistic beliefs while preserving factual QA. This reframes belief-vs-fact confusion as a temporal-indexing problem and offers a cheap, interpretable fix. All experiments run on <=9B models feasible for an academic lab.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build state-change narratives. Each item = an entity with a property that changes across K=1..3 explicitly ordered events/timestamps (e.g., 'In 2019 the museum housed the painting; in 2021 it was sold; in 2023 it was recovered'). Use factual (real-world-ish) and neutral/fictional templates to separate parametric priors from in-context state. For each narrative, generate query types: 'What is the current state of X?', 'What was the state of X at time/event t?', and belief framings ('Do you believe X is currently ...?'). Include a K=0 single-state control (no change) as the clean baseline. ~2-3k items with entity/order/timestamp randomization and controls. 2) Behavioral anachronism analysis: Query current-state and past-state beliefs; define anachronism-rate = fraction where the model reports a formerly-true (superseded) state as the current belief. Measure how anachronism-rate scales with K (number of changes), narrative length, and factual-vs-fictional content. Compare first- vs third-person and belief-vs-fact phrasings (extending KaBLE-style asymmetries to time). Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, plus a base vs chat pair. 3) Internal geometry: Extract residual-stream activations at query positions. Train linear/logistic probes for (a) the state-value assigned to X and (b) the temporal-validity index (is this the current or a past state?). Report per-layer probe accuracy and the subspace separation (principal angles / cosine) between current- and stale-belief representations. 4) Error-geometry link: Correlate per-example anachronism errors with layerwise collapse (low separation) of the current-vs-stale directions; test whether collapse predicts anachronistic answers (AUC) beyond a state-confidence baseline. 5) Causal steering: Recover a 'temporal-validity' direction via difference-of-means between current-belief and stale-belief activations; add/subtract it and measure (i) controllability (does it flip current<->past belief reports?) and (ii) specificity (does the encoded state-value or unrelated factual QA change?). Test correcting anachronistic cases by pushing toward the current-index. 6) Lightweight fix: A small LoRA fine-tune (or steering-only) with an auxiliary contrastive loss increasing current/stale separation; evaluate anachronism-rate reduction and factual QA retention (MMLU/TriviaQA subset) and temporal-QA (TimeQA/TempLAMA subset). Metrics: anachronism-rate, probe accuracy, current-vs-stale separation, prediction AUC, steering controllability & specificity, retained factual/temporal accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Stated belief may not equal internal belief; mitigated by pairing behavioral anachronism with probe-decoded state/time trajectories and reporting divergences. 2) The temporal-validity direction may be entangled with recency/position features rather than semantic time; mitigated by randomizing event order vs. narrative order and adding position controls. 3) Linear probes may miss nonlinear temporal encoding; we also try MLP probes and report negatives as informative. 4) Templated narratives may induce surface shortcuts; mitigated by paraphrase, entity/timestamp randomization, and control conditions. 5) Steering may have off-target effects on state content; specificity/retention metrics quantify this. 6) Effects may vary across model families and scale; we report per-condition rather than universal claims.
